Evaluating QAOA expectation values can be as hard as counting optimal solutions

**Abstract**

Evaluating expectation values is a critical task for variational quantum eigensolvers, parameterized quantum circuits, and many other quantum algorithms. We consider the well-studied case of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for the MaxCut problem. Recent work of Wang et al. [arXiv:2511.20212] showed this task to be NP-hard in general for any QAOA depth \(p\ge 2\), complementing past results showing efficiently computable formulas for _p_=1 with arbitrary problem graphs. We sharpen this dichotomy showing that for \(p\ge 2\) exact or exponentially precise cost expectation value evaluation is #P-hard under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. Hardness at \(p\ge 2\) is shown to remain even for evaluating single pairwise correlators \(\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle\), as well as for highly restricted sets of algorithm parameters. Our proof refines the NP-hardness construction of Wang et al. that recovers the maximum cut value from the largest exponent of a QAOA Laurent polynomial, utilizing a distinct and simpler construction that extracts a value proportional to the total number of maximum cuts, in addition to the optimal cut value. Thus we show that the QAOA expectation value hardness transition from _p_=1 to _p_=2 is not only from tractability to optimization hardness, but to that of counting optimal solutions. As an application we show our results imply analogous hardness results for computing gradients and Hessians of QAOA circuits.

## 1 Introduction

Quantum computing has attracted much interest toward enabling novel approaches to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, in both exact and approximate optimization settings [1]. At the same time, rigorous results characterizing their power or limitations remain relatively sparse, impeding our assessment of their true utility or potential for quantum advantage here. A popular paradigm is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [2,3], in particular applied to the prototypical NP-hard MaxCut problem. For analyzing quantum algorithms such as QAOA it is common to bound its expected approximation ratio in terms of the expectation value of a quantum observable encoding the cost function. This corresponds to the expected cost value of samples obtained from repeated preparation and measurement of a fixed QAOA state. For QAOA April 8, 2025 DRAFT

at its lowest depth (number of layers) _p_=1 for MaxCut, exact analytic formulas for the expected cost value were obtained in \[4\]. On the other hand, recent work of \[5\] has shown that computing the same quantities for \(p\ge 2\) is itself in general NP-hard (i.e., can be as hard as the underlying problem itself). Our main contribution is to sharpen this dichotomy to show that the \(p\ge 2\) case is in fact #P-hard; i.e., the latter case is as hard as counting the number of optimal solutions of a constraint satisfaction problem, not just finding one, which is generally believed to be a harder task \[6, 7\].

## QAOA for MaxCut

Consider the MaxCut problem on a graph _G_=(_V,E_) on _n_=|_V_| vertices. We identify cuts as spin (bit) assignments \(x\in\{\pm 1\}^n\) with cut value

\(\mathrm{c}_G(x)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\frac{1-x_ux_v}{2},\mathrm{MC}(G)=\mathrm{max}_x\mathrm{c}_G(x),\#\mathrm{MC}(G)=\{x:\mathrm{c}_G(x)=\mathrm{MC}(G)\}.\) (1)

Finding a maximum cut is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. Counting maximum cuts exactly, i.e. determining |#MC(_G_)|, is #P-hard \[8, Lemma 13\] (see also \[9, 10\]).

For QAOA applied to MaxCut we define the standard cost and mixer Hamiltonians from the single-qubit Pauli matrices \(X=(\begin{array}{ c c }
0 & 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array})\) and \(Z=(\begin{array}{ c c }
1 & 0 \\
0 & -1
\end{array})\) as<tbc>

\(C_G=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\frac{I-Z_uZ_v}{2},B=\sum_{v\in V}X_v.\) (2)

<tbc>Here _C<sub>G</sub>_ satisfies \(C_G|x\rangle=c_G(x)|x\rangle\) for every computational basis state \(|x\rangle\). At depth parameter _p_, standard QAOA for MaxCut prepares the quantum state\[11\]<tbc>

\(|\psi_p(\unknown,\unknown)\rangle=(e^{-\mathrm{i}\beta_pB}e^{-\mathrm{i}\gamma_pC_G})\dots(e^{-\mathrm{i}\beta_2B}e^{-\mathrm{i}\gamma_2C_G})(e^{-\mathrm{i}\beta_1B}e^{-\mathrm{i}\gamma_1C_G})|+\rangle^{\otimes n},\) (3)

<tbc>for easy-to-prepare initial product state \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{2^n}\), while seeking 2_p_ parameters (angles) \(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_p,\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p\) optimizing the cost expectation value

\(F_p(G;\unknown,\unknown)=\langle\psi_p|C_G|\psi_p\rangle.\) (4)

Given \(F_p(G;\unknown,\unknown)\) one can then obtain bounds on the expected approximation ratio obtained by repeatedly preparing and measuring the QAOA state with the same parameters on a quantum computer \[2, 4, 12\]. Evaluations of \(F_p(G;\unknown,\unknown)\) are also important for other algorithm aspects including parameter optimization.

The complexity of evaluating Eq. (4) is distinct from the complexity of sampling from the full QAOA output distribution \[13\]. At _p_=1, the expectation value has an explicit formula on general graphs \[2, 4\] (see Appendix A). By contrast, Wang, Chen, Sun, and Zhang recently showed \[5\] that exact evaluation is NP-hard for every fixed \(p\ge 2\). Their hardness proof writes the cost expectation as a Laurent polynomial in a phase variable and recovers MC(_G_) from its largest nonzero exponent when evaluated for \(C_{G^\prime}\) on a suitably transformed graph \(G'=G'(G)\).

The present work upgrades this mechanism for \(p\ge 2\) from optimization to counting hardness. At _p_=2, we tie the phase angles, \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\phi\), and fix the mixer angles to \(\beta_1=\mathrm{arctan}(1/2)\) and \(\beta_2=\pi/4\). This leaves a one-parameter expectation value, which is a Laurent polynomial in \(z=e^{\mathrm{i}\phi}\). We construct reduced problem instances for which the extremal Laurent polynomial coefficient can be evaluated in closed form and is shown to be proportional to the full maximum cut degeneracy |#MC(_G_)| of the input problem graph. The required coefficient property is enforced by complete bipartite subgraph _K<sub>L,L</sub>_ variable gadgets with suitably chosen _L=O(n_), along with densely<tbc>

connected anchor variables. See Figure 1 below for an illustrative example of our construction. Our main theorem uses polynomially many expectation value queries at different phase values to interpolate the required Laurent coefficient for _p_=2. This interpolation argument applies to both exact evaluation and to evaluation with exponentially small additive error. Hence we show Turing reducibility between these problems, written informally as

\(|\#\text{MC}|\le_T\text{Eval}_{p=2}^\text{MC}.\)

The general _p_ result then follows setting all angles in the additional _p_-2 layers to zero. This yields #P-hardness for computing QAOA expectation values rather than NP-hardness as in prior work. We further show that hardness remains when restricted to computing a single-edge correlator \(\langle Z_rZ_s\rangle\).

## 1.1 Main result: Evaluating QAOA _p_=2 expectation values is #P-hard

**Definition 1.1** (QAOA expectation value evaluation problem)**.** _For fixed_ \(p\in\mathbb{N}\)_, let_ \(\text{Eval}_p^\text{MC}\) _be the function problem that maps a graph G and parameters_ \(\unknown,\unknown\) _to the exact algebraic number_<tbc>

\(F_p(G;\unknown,\unknown).\)

<tbc>_The additive-error version additionally receives_ \(b\in\mathbb{N}\) _in unary\[14\] and returns a rational number_ \(\widetilde{F}\) _satisfying_<tbc>

\(\left|\widetilde{F}-F_p(G;\unknown,\unknown)\right|\le 2^{-b}.\)

<tbc>For a designated edge \(e=\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), we additionally define

\(\text{Eval}_p^\text{uv}(G;\unknown,\unknown):=\langle\psi_p|Z_uZ_v|\psi_p\rangle.\)

We will primarily be concerned with deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions, i.e., what one can solve efficiently given a black box computing \(\text{Eval}_p^\text{MC}\). The output of an exact evaluation oracle is understood to be expressed in a standard basis of the compositum of the number fields in which the input is represented. The particular numerical representation is inessential for the Turing reductions below, provided it supports polynomial-time exact arithmetic and basis conversion. Every oracle (subroutine) query uses a number field of polynomial degree and the inverse Fourier transform is carried out exactly within that field. QAOA angles are specified exactly by algebraic values of their sines and cosines; the reduction uses only roots of unity and fixed algebraic values for the sines and cosines of the mixer angles.\[15\] The explicit number field representation is specified in Appendix B.

Here FP denotes the class of functions computable by a deterministic classical algorithm in time polynomial in the input length.

**Theorem 1.2** (QAOA expectation complexity dichotomy)**.** _For unweighted simple graphs,_

\(\text{Eval}_1^\text{MC}\in\mathsf{FP},\) (5)

\(\text{Eval}_p^\text{MC}\text{\textit{is}}\#P\text{\textit{-hard for every fixed}}p\ge 2.\) (6)

_Moreover, for every fixed_ \(p\ge 2\)_, it suffices to restrict evaluations to QAOA angles_

\(\gamma_1=\gamma_2,\beta_1=arctan\frac{1}{2},\beta_2=\frac{\pi}{4},\gamma_j=\beta_j=0(3\le j\le p).\) (7)

**Corollary 1.3.** _The same conclusions of the theorem hold if the oracle evaluates only one designated two-qubit correlator_ \(\langle Z_rZ_s\rangle\) _rather than the global cost expectation value_ \(\langle C_G\rangle\).

Here the mixer angles are fixed constants independent of the input, and only the single tied cost phase angle \(\phi:=\gamma_1=\gamma_2\) is varied between oracle queries.

Appendix B strengthens the exact-evaluation statement to a single oracle query. That reduction builds on the construction of Theorem 1.2 and requires additional algebraic steps to recover the Laurent coefficients from one exact output. It also shows hardness for the symmetric fixed choice \(\beta_1=\beta_2=\pi/4\) of mixing angles after adding at most one isolated source vertex. This single-query reduction is algebraic rather than necessarily numerically robust; the polynomial interpolation using Fourier recovery in the main proof remains the stable route for additive approximation.

We show the hardness dichotomy of the theorem extends directly to the setting of exponentially small additive error in Section 2.3.

**Remark 1.4** (Consequences of efficient exact evaluation)**.** _Suppose that, for_ \(p\ge 2\)_, the exact or exponentially precise expectation value of the MaxCut QAOA circuit can be computed in polynomial time on arbitrary graphs. Then by Toda’s theorem [16] the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its lowest level, i.e. P=PH._

For exponentially precise evaluation, we show below that, for an _N_-vertex oracle instance, the extreme Laurent coefficient has magnitude at least 2<sup>-_cN_</sup> for a known constant _c_, and hence _O(N_) bits of additive precision suffice to recover the exact integer count by rounding.

We emphasize that both our results and those of Ref. [5] imply that there exist worst-case families of graphs for which evaluating _F<sub>p</sub>_ appears computationally intractable, but this by no means implies this property applies to all graphs. Indeed, Ref. [5] establishes complementary algorithms parameterized by local treewidth [5], complementing results obtained for other special cases for which rigorous results have been obtained in the literature [2,4,12,17-31]. Furthermore, whether one can efficiently estimate a given QAOA cost expectation value on a classical computer or not, a quantum computer may still be required to obtain corresponding problem solution samples [13].

## 1.2 Relationship to the results of [5] and related work

Prior to [5], a sequence of papers [2,4,12,17-22,24-31] obtained formulas or bounds for \(\text{Eval}_p^\text{MC}\) in special cases. Beyond performance analysis, evaluating QAOA expectation values is also critical for algorithm parameter selection; in [32] it was shown that the parameter optimization problem in some settings can itself become NP-hard.

For computing QAOA expectation values, Reference [5] previously established NP-hardness for every fixed \(p\ge 2\) by identifying the maximum cut value with the largest nonzero exponent of a Laurent polynomial. Here we retain the general Laurent polynomial approach but replace the underlying graph construction with one that utilizes a balanced counting gadget, and for this graph prove a corresponding exact leading coefficient identity. The new balanced gadgets make every maximum cut of the constructed _N_-vertex graph have Hamming distance _N/_2 from each assignment maximizing the cut decrease when the two anchors are flipped, so all such cuts contribute the same known weight to the leading coefficient. This property yields a count, rather than only the optimal value. The resulting new conclusions are: (i) #P-hardness through recovery of the number of maximum cuts; (ii) hardness for a single edge correlator; and (iii) the fixed-angle restrictions of Theorem 1.2. Our analysis is primarily concerned with the _p_=2 case. The \(p\ge 2\) statement then follows by padding a hard depth-two circuit with _p_-2 identity layers (i.e., layers for which \(\gamma=\beta=0\)).

Our results apply instead to computation of QAOA expectation values; these quantities can also be estimated _quantumly_ by repeated sampling from the quantum computer. In [13] Farhi and Harrow adapted the postselection-based framework of [33] to show that efficient classical<tbc>

<tbc>sampling from the output of standard QAOA circuits even at depth _p_=1 would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy (to at least its third level), with this result further sharpened in the recent paper [34]. Krovi later proved average-case hardness results [35] for approximating output probabilities of random quantum circuits, including random _p_=1 QAOA ensembles. In [36] the authors refine asymptotic supremacy arguments into a fine-grained framework, allowing quantitative statements about the scale required for classical intractability based on standard conjectures in complexity theory. Hence in terms of sampling tasks, QAOA circuits provide a potential path to quantum computational supremacy [13, 36, 37]. Our complementary results show a stronger conditional collapse of the polynomial hierarchy to PH=P if one could efficiently evaluate QAOA expectation values (to exponential precision), but with distinct threshold _p_=2.

Our result should also be distinguished from work on more general quantum mean value problems for constant-depth circuits [38]. In that setting, depth refers to physical circuit depth in a local gate model, and substantially broader circuit and observable families are considered. By contrast the fixed parameter _p_ in our theorems counts QAOA rounds. As the graphs produced by our reduction contain universal vertices, a standard two-qubit-gate implementation of a cost layer has depth \(\Omega(N)\); consequently, our theorem is not a hardness result for constant physical-depth circuits. Its novelty is instead that exact #P-hardness already occurs within the rigid family of standard fixed-round MaxCut-QAOA circuits, with either the MaxCut Hamiltonian or one designated two-qubit correlator as the observable. Moreover, our proof is qualitatively different, deriving hardness directly from an extreme Laurent-polynomial coefficient rather than from postselection-induced universality [33, 38]. On the other hand, our theorem concerns exact, or exponentially precise, evaluation and therefore does not establish hardness in the constant-additive-error regime considered in Ref. [38].

Further afield, Szegedy [39] previously proposed viewing QAOA expectation values as graph invariants, and investigated whether structural information such as graph non-isomorphism can be recovered from comparing these quantities. Distinct from the expectation value setting, in [40] it was shown that #P-hardness can arise in the construction of Hamiltonian representations for compactly specified Boolean functions. Complementary work establishes complexity barriers to efficiently preparing states whose measured solutions recover a fixed positive fraction of the optimal MaxCut gain over a random cut on every input [41] and to optimizing Hamiltonians compressed by quantum random access optimization [42]. Here we study the complexity of evaluating expectation values for specified QAOA circuits. QAOA has also been proposed as a solution sampler for approximate counting [43]. Finally, we note that beyond [5], Laurent polynomials have also proven useful in two recent works solving QAOA for MaxCut on the special case of "ring of disagrees" (two-regular graphs) [44, 45], confirming optimal expected cost scaling with _p_ originally conjectured in [2].

The following section gives the details and proof of Theorem 1.2. We show a direct application of our results to assessing the hardness of computing gradients and Hessians for QAOA circuits in Sec. 3, and provide some additional discussion of our results in Section 4.

## 2 A balanced maximum-cut counting gadget

To encode the maximum cuts of an input graph _H_, we replace each vertex by a balanced complete bipartite gadget. In every maximum cut of the resulting graph _G_, each gadget’s two parts lie on opposite sides, and their orientations specify a maximum cut of _H_ (Lemma 2.1). Two anchor vertices, joined to every other vertex, make their shared edge the sole contributor to the largest Laurent exponent at depth two (Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3). The balance ensures that every maximum cut contributes the same weight to the corresponding coefficient, making it a known nonzero multiple of |#MC(_H_)| at our chosen mixer angles (Theorem 2.4). Polynomial interpolation using Fourier recovery then yields the count (Section 2.2).

Let input graph _H_=(_V,E_) have _n_ vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). Define the odd integer

\(L=2(\Delta+2)+1.\) (8)

For each \(v\in V(H)\), introduce disjoint vertex sets _A<sub>v</sub>_={_a_<sub>_v,_1</sub>_,...,a<sub>v,L</sub>_} and _B<sub>v</sub>_, each of size _L_, and add all edges of the complete bipartite graph between them. For each \(\{u,w\}\in E(H)\) and each \(j\in[L]\), add the synchronous edge {_a<sub>u,j</sub>,a<sub>w,j</sub>_} connecting the corresponding vertices in _A<sub>u</sub>_ and _A<sub>w</sub>_. (Synchronous edges are not added for vertices in the _B<sub>v</sub>_.) Finally add two anchor vertices _r,s_, the edge _e<sub>⋆</sub>_={_r,s_}, and join each anchor to every vertex in

\(W=\bigcup_{v\in V(H)}(A_v\cup B_v).\) (9)

Denote the resulting graph by _G_=G(_H_). It is unweighted, simple, and connected, with

\(N:=|V(G)|=2nL+2\) (10)

vertices. The number of edges is

\(|E(G)|=nL^2+L|E(H)|+4nL+1.\) (11)

Since \(\Delta\le n-1\), we have _L=O(n_), and hence _N_=|_V(G_)|=_O(n_<sup>2</sup>) and |_E(G_)|=_O(n_<sup>3</sup>). Thus G(_H_), and all oracle queries generated from it, can be constructed in polynomial time.

The following lemma shows that every maximum cut of _G_ encodes a maximum cut of _H_, and that each maximum cut of _H_ has exactly two lifts to _G_.

**Lemma 2.1** (Gadget rigidity)**.** _Every maximum cut of G places each A<sub>v</sub> and B<sub>v</sub> monochromatically on opposite sides, places r and s on opposite sides, and induces a maximum cut of H through the orientation of the sets A<sub>v</sub>. Conversely, every maximum cut of H and either orientation of_ (_r,s_) _determine a maximum cut of G. Consequently,_

\(\mathrm{MC}(G)=nL^2+2nL+1+L\mathrm{MC}(H),\) (12)

\(|\#\mathrm{MC}(G)|=2|\#\mathrm{MC}(H)|.\) (13)

_Moreover every maximum cut contains exactly_ |_W|/_2=_nL vertices of W on each side._

_Proof._ Each vertex of a variable _K<sub>L,L</sub>_ has at most \(\Delta+2\) external neighbors. Consider one variable gadget with parts _A<sub>v</sub>_ and _B<sub>v</sub>_. Its two proper orientations assign +1 to all of _A<sub>v</sub>_ and -1 to all of _B<sub>v</sub>_, or the reverse. Choose the orientation at minimum Hamming distance from the current labeling, allowing either choice in a tie. Relative to this choice, let _a_ vertices of _A<sub>v</sub>_ and _b_ vertices of _B<sub>v</sub>_ be misplaced, and set _q=a+b_. The Hamming distances from the current labeling of \(A_v\cup B_v\) to the two proper bipartite orientations sum to 2_L_. Therefore the nearer orientation has Hamming distance \(q\le L\). The number of cut edges internal to the gadget is<tbc>

\((L-a)(L-b)+ab=L^2-Lq+2ab.\)

<tbc>Thus correcting the orientation of the gadget gains at least

\(Lq-2ab\ge Lq-\frac{q^2}{2}\ge\frac{Lq}{2}\)

internal cut edges, where we used \(2ab\le q^2/2\) and \(q\le L\). Each moved vertex has at most \(\Delta+2\) external neighbors, so this correction loses at most \((\Delta+2)q\) external cut edges. This bound counts incidences between moved vertices and external edges; an external edge incident to two moved vertices may therefore be counted twice, but this is harmless for an upper bound. Since \(L>2(\Delta+2)\), the net change is strictly positive whenever _q\>_0. Consequently every maximum cut orients each _K<sub>L,L</sub>_ gadget properly. Thus each gadget contributes _L_<sup>2</sup> cut edges and exactly _L_ vertices to each side.

If the anchors lie on the same side, flipping one anchor leaves the total number of cut anchor-_W_ edges unchanged, because _W_ is balanced, and additionally cuts {_r,s_}. Hence the anchors are opposite. With opposite anchors, every \(w\in W\) contributes exactly one cut anchor edge. The only orientation-dependent edges are the synchronous edges: the _L_ edges representing \(\{u,v\}\in E(H)\) are cut exactly when the orientations of _A<sub>u</sub>_ and _A<sub>v</sub>_ differ. The gadget and anchor edges contribute the fixed amount _nL_<sup>2</sup>+2_nL_+1, while the synchronous edges contribute _L_ times the encoded cut value in _H_. Maximizing the cut of _G_ therefore maximizes this encoded cut, giving (12). Finally, each labeled maximum cut of _H_ determines every gadget spin, and the two anchor orientations give exactly two lifts, proving (13).

Our graph construction is simpler and more symmetric than the gadget used in Ref. \[5\]. The latter employs asymmetric complete-bipartite vertex gadgets, a separate large complete-bipartite frame, and an additional controller vertex in order to isolate the maximal Laurent exponent. By contrast, our reduction uses only balanced (_K<sub>L,L</sub>_) variable gadgets and two universal anchors (r,s).<tbc>

## 2.1 The extreme coefficient at depth two Fix an edge _e_={_u,v_} of a graph _G_. Set \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\phi\), \(\beta_1=\beta\), \(\beta_2=\pi/4\), and define \(H_e(e^{\mathrm{i}\phi},\beta):=\langle\psi_2(\phi,\phi;\beta,\pi/4)|Z_uZ_v|\psi_2(\phi,\phi;\beta,\pi/4)\rangle.\) (14) For \(a,b\in\{\pm 1\}\) let \(K_\beta^\pm(a,b)=\langle a|e^{\pm\mathrm{i}\beta X}|b\rangle\). Writing \(c=\mathrm{cos}\beta\) and \(s=\mathrm{sin}\beta\) we have \(K_\beta^\pm(a,b)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } c, & a=b, \\ \pm\mathrm{is}, & a\neq b, \end{array}\right.\) (15) Let _Te_ operate on an assignment string so as to flip the two vertex spins in _e_. The next lemma rewrites the edge correlator as a sum of powers of the phase factor, which lets us analyze its coefficients. The proof uses a sum-over-paths expansion over intermediate computational-basis states, as in earlier analyses of QAOA circuits \[5, 25, 27\]. **Lemma 2.2** (Reduced path sum)**.** _For_ \(z=e^{\mathrm{i}\phi}\), \(H_e(z;\beta)=-2^{-N}\sum_{x,y,t\in\{\pm 1\}^{V(G)}}y_uy_vz^{\mathrm{c}_G(x)-\mathrm{c}_G(t)+\mathrm{c}_G(y)-\mathrm{c}_G(T_ey)}\)
\(\times\prod_{w\in V(G)}K_\beta^+(x_w,y_w)K_\beta^-((T_ey)_w,t_w).\) (16) _Hence_ \(H_e(z;\beta)\) _is a Laurent polynomial in z._ _Proof._ Write \(|s\rangle\) for the computational-basis state labeled by a spin string \(s\in\{\pm 1\}^{V(G)}\), and insert \(I=\sum_s|s\rangle\langle s|\) between successive operators in the QAOA expectation value. Label the strings at the first and second cost layers on the bra (complex-conjugate) side by _x,y_, and on the ket side by \(t,\bar{y}\), respectively. Here \(\bar{y}\) is an independent label, not the spin complement of _y_. Let _q_ label the basis state at the observable _ZuZv_, whose eigenvalue is _quqv_. The diagonal cost layers supply the four cut-value phases below; the two overlaps with the uniform initial state supply 2-_N_. Since \(B=\sum_wX_w\), the mixer matrix elements factor over vertices, giving \(H_e(z;\beta)=2^{-N}\sum_{x,y,\bar{y},t,q\in\{\pm 1\}^{V(G)}}q_qu_vz^{\mathrm{c}_G(x)-\mathrm{c}_G(t)+\mathrm{c}_G(y)-\mathrm{c}_G(\bar{y})}\)
\(\times\prod_{w\in V(G)}K_\beta^+(x_w,y_w)K_\bar{\beta}^-(\bar{y}_w,t_w)\prod_{w\in V(G)}K_{\pi/4}^+(y_w,q_w)K_{\pi/4}^-(q_w,\bar{y}_w).\) Summing over the intermediate spins adjacent to the final mixer gives, for \(w\notin e\), \(\sum_{q_w}K_{\pi/4}^+(y_w,q_w)K_{\pi/4}^-(q_w,\bar{y}_w)=\delta_{y_w,\bar{y}_w},\) (17) and, for \(w\in e\), \(\sum_{q_w}q_wK_{\pi/4}^+(y_w,q_w)K_{\pi/4}^-(q_w,\bar{y}_w)=-\mathrm{i}y_w\delta_{\bar{y}_w,-y_w}.\) (18) The two endpoint factors multiply to (-i_yu_)(-i_yv_)=-_yuyv_. The Kronecker deltas enforce \(\bar{y}=T_ey\), giving (16). Define the largest possible cut-value decrease from flipping both endpoints of _e_: \(R_e=\mathrm{max}_y\big[\mathrm{c}_G(y)-\mathrm{c}_G(T_ey)\big].\) (19)

The next lemma determines the largest possible decrease in cut value caused by flipping both endpoints of an edge. This bounds the term c_G(y_)-c_G(Tey_) in the correlator’s Laurent exponents. **Lemma 2.3** (Largest cut decrease)**.** _For every edge e_={_u,v_} _of a simple graph, let du and dv denote the degrees of u and v, respectively. Then_ \(R_e=d_u+d_v-2.\) (20) _Proof._ Only edges incident on exactly one endpoint can change when both endpoints are flipped, so \(R_e\le d_u+d_v-2\). Equality is attained by assigning the same spin to _u,v_ and the opposite spin to every other neighbor of either endpoint. This assignment is consistent even when _u_ and _v_ have common neighbors, since every vertex in \((N(u)\cup N(v))\backslash\{u,v\}\) receives the same spin opposite to _u_ and _v_. For the anchor edge _e⋆_={_r,s_} of _G_=G(_H_), both endpoints are universal and therefore \(R_{e_\star}=2N-4.\) (21) The only assignments attaining _Re⋆_ are \((q_\sigma)_r=(q_\sigma)_s=\sigma,(q_\sigma)_w=-\sigma(w\in W),\sigma\in\{\pm 1\},\) (22) for which \(T_{e_\star} q_\sigma=-\sigma\mathbf{1}\). Since every nonanchor vertex has degree strictly less than _N_-1, _e⋆_ uniquely maximizes _Re_ among all edges. ## Hardness on diameter-two graphs

**Corollary 2.6.** _For every fixed_ \(p\ge 2\)_, exact evaluation of the MaxCut QAOA expectation is_ #P_-hard under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions, even when restricted to connected, unweighted, simple graphs of diameter two. The same conclusion holds for the expectation of the designated two-qubit observable Z<sub>r</sub>Z<sub>s</sub>, where_ {_r,s_} _is an edge joining two universal vertices._

_Proof._ The graph G(_H_) constructed in the proof of Theorem 1.2 is unweighted, simple, and connected. The two anchor vertices _r_ and _s_ are adjacent to one another and to every vertex in every variable gadget. Let \(u,v\in V(\mathcal{G}(H))\). If neither vertex is _r_, then both are adjacent to _r_, and hence there is a path _u-r-v_ of length at most two. If one of the vertices is _r_, then the pair is adjacent. Thus every pair of distinct vertices is joined by a path of length at most two, so \(\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{G}(H))\le 2\). The graph is not complete: for example, two distinct vertices in the same part _A<sub>v</sub>_ of a variable gadget _K<sub>L,L</sub>_ are nonadjacent. Hence diam(G(_H_))=2.

**Remark 2.7.** _The diameter-two restriction is obtained at the expense of large degree that scales with the problem size, as it must: any diameter-two graph on N vertices has maximum degree at least_ \(\sqrt{N-1}\) _(because from any vertex, at most_ \(1+\Delta+\Delta(\Delta-1)=\Delta^2+1\) _vertices can lie within distance two). Each anchor is adjacent to every gadget vertex, and the vertices within each K<sub>L,L</sub> gadget have degree growing with the source-instance input problem size. Consequently, the corollary does not establish hardness for bounded-degree graph families._

\(=2^{1-N}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{N/2}\frac{2^N-1}{5^{N/2}}\)
\(\ge\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}\right)^N=2^{-N\mathrm{log}_2(5/\sqrt{2})}.\) (35) Here we used the triangle inequality and \(2^N-1\ge 2^{N-1}\). ## 4 Discussion

Our main theorem gives a clean exact-complexity classification by depth for the standard QAOA for MaxCut expectation values on unrestricted graphs: _p_=1 is polynomial-time computable, whereas every fixed \(p\ge 2\) is already #P-hard. Our reduction uses high-degree anchors, consistent with the tractability of fixed-depth cost expectation value evaluation on bounded-degree or bounded-local- treewidth graph families \[5\]. This degree dependence differs sharply from that of the full-distribution sampling problem: for general 2-local cost Hamiltonians, \(\bar{\text{Åbolin}}\) and Ambainis \[34\] recently showed that depth-one QAOA sampling is already classically hard for multiplicative-error sampling at interaction (maximum vertex) degree three, whereas degree-two instances are exactly classically sampleable in polynomial time for _p=O_(log_n_). Thus the relevant degree threshold depends essentially on whether the classical task is evaluation of a local or global expectation value or sampling from the complete QAOA output distribution. Our reduction also concerns exact or exponentially precise algebraic evaluation; no claims are made about computations outputting constant or polynomially small error.

Our main result is worst-case and does not imply hardness for all or for typical graphs (MaxCut problem instances). An interesting future direction is a more precise characterization of which graph subfamilies our hardness obstruction applies to or not. As mentioned, analytic or numerical solutions are possible in a number of cases. For example, a sequence of papers has obtained successively improved results concerning QAOA for MaxCut on high-girth graphs \[4, 20-23, 27, 46, 47\], where our present reduction does not apply. A particularly important open direction is to determine to what degree computational hardness of QAOA expectation values persists at physically relevant levels of precision, in particular for constant or inverse-polynomial additive error, as well as under physical noise \[48-50\]. Related numerical studies show that finite sampling and noise in objective function evaluations can place severe resource demands on variational optimization \[51, 52\]. These results concern training and measurement costs rather than the classical complexity of expectation- value evaluation studied here. Resolving this question would help clarify the extent to which the exact-complexity transition at _p_=2 constrains efficient quantum or classical evaluation of QAOA expectation values, both theoretically and in practice. Similar considerations apply to related quantities such as their gradients and Hessians important for parameter optimization.

### Implications for algorithms based on QAOA expectation values

Recently a number of hybrid approaches have been proposed based on classical processing of quantum expectation values obtained using a quantum ansatz such as QAOA. Examples include so-called Iterative Quantum Algorithms \[19, 53-58\], where correlators \(\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle\) are iteratively estimated and processed to obtain a sequence of reduced problem instances, and related relaxation-based approaches \[59, 60\], where the expectation values are classically processed to produce candidate solutions directly. Strengthening the implications of \[5\], Theorem 1.2 shows that the expectation values appearing in these and other<tbc>

<tbc>related approaches can be computationally hard to evaluate in the worst case, at least if exponential precision is required; we point the reader to \[58, Sec. III.D\] for additional relevant discussion. Our present results neither establish nor rule out potential quantum advantage for these algorithms.

#### Connections to quantum supremacy experiments

Our main result provides an expectation value analogue of existing sampling-hardness results for low-depth QAOA circuits \[13, 36, 37\]. Already at QAOA depth _p_=2, we show classical evaluation of a restricted QAOA for MaxCut expectation value suffices to recover #P-hard counting information. However, this does not by itself constitute an experimentally accessible quantum-advantage result. In particular, by Hoeffding’s inequality, estimating an edge correlator with measurement outcomes in \(\{\pm 1\}\) to additive error \(\varepsilon\) using independent circuit measurements can be achieved with \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}log\frac{1}{\delta})\) independent samples to achieve failure probability at most \(\delta\). For the global MaxCut observable, a computational basis measurement instead returns a cut value in \[0_,m_\], where _m_=|_E(G_)|. Directly estimating the unnormalized expectation \(\langle C_G\rangle\) to additive error \(\varepsilon\) can be achieved with \(O(m^2\varepsilon^{-2}log\frac{1}{\delta})\) samples. At the accuracy \(\varepsilon=2^{-\alpha N}\) used in our reduction, these standard direct-sampling bounds are exponential; the additional _m_<sup>2</sup>=poly(_N_) factor for the global objective doesn’t change this scaling. Our result should consequently be interpreted as a structural worst-case statement about QAOA expectation value landscapes, rather than as one concerning experimentally accessible precision.

With \(d=[K:\mathbb{Q}]\), each value \(a_0+a_1\theta+\cdots+a_{d-1}\theta^{d-1}\) is represented by its list of rational basis coefficients (_a_0_,...,a__d_-1), encoded in binary. The input supplies such lists for i, for each cost phase \(z_j=e^{\mathrm{i}\gamma_j}\), and for each mixer pair \((c_j,s_j)=(\mathrm{cos}\beta_j,\mathrm{sin}\beta_j)\). The input is promised to satisfy |_zj_|=1, \(c_j,s_j\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(c_j^2+s_j^2=1\) under that embedding. The exact oracle returns the coefficient list of the expectation value in the same field and basis. Input and output lengths are the respective total bit lengths of these presentations and coefficient lists. Other exact encodings give the same conclusions whenever conversion to and from this representation is polynomial time. This qualification matters for the one-query statement below. Write \(\zeta_t=e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}/t}\) for the primitive _t_-th root of unity. The one-query construction uses the common field \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_8,\zeta_q)=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{8q})\), where _q_ is an odd prime chosen in the proof. This field has degree 4(_q_-1); its polynomial bit-length bound is verified in the proof.
With the representation above and equal fixed mixers, one exact oracle answer suffices for the counting reduction. **Theorem B.1** (Single-query fixed-mixer hardness)**.** _Under the explicit number field representation above, for every fixed_ \(p\ge 2\)_, exact evaluation of the MaxCut QAOA expectation is_ #P_-hard under a deterministic polynomial-time reduction making one oracle call. This remains true for the designated_

<tbc>_correlator_ \(\langle Z_rZ_s\rangle\) _and for connected, unweighted, simple graphs of diameter two. At depth two the hard instances may be restricted to_

\(\beta_1=\beta_2=\frac{\pi}{4},\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\phi,e^{\mathrm{i}\phi}=\zeta_q,\) (38)

_where_ \(\zeta_q\) _has polynomial order. For p\>_2_, all later angles may be set to zero._

_Proof._ We use the explicit one-query hardness reduction for counting maximum cuts in simple graphs given by Dell et al. \[64, full version, Lemmas C.2-C.3\]. Given a source graph _H_ with _n_ vertices, set<tbc>

\(\widehat{H}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
H, & n\mathrm{odd}, \\
H\sqcup K_1, & n\mathrm{even},
\end{array}\right.\rho=|V(\widehat{H})|-n\in\{0,1\}.\) (39)

<tbc>Then \(\widehat{n}=|V(\widehat{H})|\) is odd, \(\mathrm{MC}(\widehat{H})=\mathrm{MC}(H)\), and \(|\#\mathrm{MC}(\widehat{H})|=2^\rho|\#\mathrm{MC}(H)|\). Apply the construction of Section 2 to \(\widehat{H}\). Because both \(\widehat{n}\) and _L_ are odd, the resulting graph \(G=\mathcal{G}(\widehat{H})\) satisfies

\(N=2\widehat{n}L+2\equiv 0(\mathrm{mod}4),|\#\mathrm{MC}(G)|=2^{\rho+1}|\#\mathrm{MC}(H)|.\) (40)

It retains all graph restrictions in the theorem.

Set \(\beta_1=\beta_2=\pi/4\) and write the anchor correlator as \(H_{e_\star}(z)=\sum_{k=-2m}^{2m}a_kz^k\), where _m_=|_E(G_)|. Theorem 2.4 and \(N\equiv 0(\mathrm{mod}4)\) give

\(a_{D_\star}=-|\#\mathrm{MC}(G)|2^{2-2N}\mathrm{i}^{N/2}\neq 0.\) (41)

For the global expectation, Eq. (30) gives the corresponding coefficient -_a_<sub>_D<sub>⋆</sub>_</sub>/2. Thus either coefficient determines |#MC(_G_)|.

All Laurent coefficients lie in \(K_0=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_8)\). Bertrand’s postulate gives an odd prime 4_m_+1_\<q\<_2(4_m_+1), so _q=O(m_). Such a prime can be found in polynomial time by testing integers in this interval. For the query field, take \(K=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)\) with \(\theta=\zeta_{8q}\) and cyclotomic defining polynomial \(\Phi_{8q}\). This polynomial has degree 4(_q_-1) and coefficients in \(\{0,\pm 1\}\), and isolating data for the chosen root can be computed with polynomial bit complexity. Encode the phases and mixers using \(z=\theta^8\), \(\mathrm{i}=\theta^{2q}\), and \(c_j=s_j=(\theta^q+\theta^{7q})/2\) for _j_=1,2, reducing powers modulo \(\Phi_{8q}\). These input lists have polynomial total bit length. Query once at \(z=\zeta_q\). Since gcd(8_,q_)=1,<tbc>

\([K:K_0]=q-1>4m.\) (42)

<tbc>Consequently \(1,\zeta_q,\dots,\zeta_q^{4m}\) are linearly independent over _K_<sub>0</sub>, and

\(\zeta_q^{2m}P(\zeta_q)=\sum_{j=0}^{4m}[z^{j-2m}]P(z)\zeta_q^j\) (43)

for either _P=H<sub>e<sub>⋆</sub></sub>_ or the global expectation. Multiply the returned value by \(\zeta_q^{2m}\) and convert its rational coordinates to the basis \(\{\zeta_8^r\zeta_q^j:0\le r<4,0\le j<q-1\}\) of _K_. Grouping the four coordinates at each _j_ gives the _K_<sub>0</sub>-coefficient \[_z_<sup>_j_-2_m_</sup>\]_P(z_) for \(0\le j\le 4m\). All remaining groups are zero. This recovers every Laurent coefficient from the single answer. The basis conversion uses polynomial-time exact linear algebra in degree 4(_q_-1)=_O(m_).

For the bit-length bound, each path in Eq. (16) at these mixer angles contributes 2<sup>-2_N_</sup> times one of \(\{\pm 1,\pm\mathrm{i}\}\) to a Laurent coefficient. There are at most 2<sup>3_N_</sup> summands, so each Laurent coefficient of the correlator has _O(N_)-bit rational coordinates in Q(i). Summing over edges gives _O(N_+log_m_)-bit coordinates for the global expectation. Substitution of \(\zeta_q\) and reduction in the<tbc>

<tbc>cyclotomic power basis preserve polynomial bit length. Thus the exact answer and its decoded coefficients have polynomial total length, and the decoding takes polynomial time. The largest exponent with a nonzero coefficient identifies _D<sub>⋆</sub>_. Equations (41) and (40) then recover |#MC(_H_)|. Zeroing later layers as before proves the claim for _p\>_2.

The final remark identifies the representation and precision limitations of the one-query proof.

**Remark B.2.** _The one-query result uses the explicit number field representation above. It also holds for exact encodings that allow polynomial-time conversion to and from these basis coefficients, but is not claimed for arbitrary exact algebraic encodings. The proof uses exact outputs and gives no O(N_)_-bit replacement for the Fourier argument in Section 2.3. Whether substantially higher precision permits algebraic reconstruction from a single value is a separate question. The decoding argument does not require padding. With the main-text mixer choices_ \(\mathrm{tan}\beta_1=1/2\) _and_ \(\beta_2=\pi/4\)_, the coefficients lie in the fixed field_ \(\mathbb{Q}(\mathrm{i},\sqrt{2},\sqrt{5})\subseteq\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{40})\)_. Choosing q coprime to_ 40 _gives the same one-query conclusion on the unpadded graph_ G(_H). The padding above is used only to obtain equal mixer angles._
